questions.stem: Which statement defines the speed of an object?

options.text: The distance an object travels every second
options.explanation: Speed counts distance covered per second, with no direction attached.

options.text: The direction an object moves in every second
options.explanation: Direction is the property of a vector; speed deliberately ignores it.

options.text: The force an object exerts every second
options.explanation: Force is a different quantity altogether and plays no part in the definition.

options.text: The total journey length regardless of time taken
options.explanation: Distance alone ignores the time; speed always brings the second dimension in.

questions.stem: Why is speed described as a scalar quantity?

options.text: It has magnitude but no direction
options.explanation: Scalar means size only; speed says how fast, never which way.

options.text: It has direction but no magnitude
options.explanation: That pairing is backwards; a direction without a size describes nothing physical here.

options.text: It always points along the path of motion
options.explanation: Pointing is vector behaviour; speed carries no arrow at all.

options.text: It can only take negative values
options.explanation: Speeds are quoted as positive magnitudes on this course.

questions.stem: How is the average speed across a whole journey calculated?

options.text: Total distance moved divided by total time taken
options.explanation: The average shares the whole distance out across the whole time.

options.text: Total distance moved multiplied by total time taken
options.explanation: Multiplying inflates the number; the relationship divides.

options.text: Final speed added to the starting speed
options.explanation: Adding endpoint readings is not the journey-wide average.

options.text: Total time taken divided by total distance moved
options.explanation: That is the reciprocal — it would answer hours per kilometre, not the speed.

questions.stem: In the formula triangle for average speed, two quantities sit on the same horizontal line. What does that mean?

options.text: They are multiplied together
options.explanation: Same-line neighbours multiply; the covered corner then leaves a division instead.

options.text: They are divided
options.explanation: Division belongs to the stacked pair, not the shared line.

options.text: They are added together
options.explanation: Nothing in the triangle is ever added; it only stores the relationship's shape.

options.text: They cancel each other out
options.explanation: Cancellation is an algebra step, not a triangle rule.

questions.stem: A hiker averages 2.0 m/s and a bee 4.5 m/s. What kind of value is each figure?

options.text: The total distance covered divided by the total time taken
options.explanation: Both figures are journey-wide averages, exactly what the relationship delivers.

options.text: The speed measured at the end of the journey only
options.explanation: An ending reading is instantaneous and says nothing about the whole trip.

options.text: The largest speed reached at any single moment
options.explanation: Peaks and averages differ; the bee's top sprint exceeds 4.5 m/s.

options.text: The direction of travel held throughout the journey
options.explanation: Direction plays no part — these are scalar averages.

questions.stem: State, in words, the relationship used to work out how fast an object moves across a whole journey.
questions.modelAnswer: average speed = total distance moved ÷ total time taken.

questions.stem: A hiker covers a six-kilometre trail in ninety minutes. Name the single quantity that summarises how fast the hiker moved overall.
questions.modelAnswer: The hiker's average speed — the total distance moved divided by the total time taken.

questions.stem: Explain why a quantity that has a magnitude but no direction cannot be classed as a vector.
questions.modelAnswer: Because a vector must carry both magnitude and direction; a quantity with magnitude alone is a scalar, and speed is exactly such a quantity.
